sections.title: Upper GI bleeding: causes and how common they are

blocks.text: Upper GI bleeding comes from a source **above the ligament of Treitz**. Acute upper GI haemorrhage is the **most frequent GI emergency**: about 50–170 hospital admissions per 100 000 people a year in the UK, with roughly **1 in 10** admitted patients dying.

blocks.title: Causes of acute upper GI haemorrhage (Davidson frequencies)
rows: NSAIDs/aspirin, _H. pylori_; the leading cause of serious, life-threatening bleeding
Usually slow ooze rather than torrential bleeding

blocks.title: Drugs and bleeding risk
items: Aspirin, **even at 75 mg a day**, and other NSAIDs cause ulcers and erosions that bleed — often in elderly patients who may not realise they take them.
Corticosteroids alone barely change bleeding risk, but **a steroid plus an NSAID** raises it synergistically.
Anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs do not create a lesion; they make bleeding from **any** existing lesion heavier.

blocks.title: Specific lesions to recognise
items: **Mallory–Weiss tear**: a linear mucosal split at the oesophagogastric junction caused by a sudden rise in intra-abdominal pressure — classically retching or alcoholic ‘dry heaves’. Vomiting _before_ the haematemesis is the clue. Most stop on their own and patients usually go home within 24 h.

**Varices**: mostly in the lowest 3–5 cm of the oesophagus, just above the junction with the stomach, or in the stomach itself. Bleeding is more likely with large varices, red spots or stripes, high portal pressure and liver failure.
**Portal hypertensive (‘snakeskin’) gastropathy**: punctate erythema from chronic gastric congestion; it more often causes repeated minor bleeding and iron deficiency than an acute bleed.
**Dieulafoy lesion**: an unusually large (1–3 mm) submucosal artery protruding through the gastric fundus mucosa; causes sudden massive bleeding and is easily missed at endoscopy.

blocks.title: Rarer causes
items: **GAVE (‘watermelon stomach’)**: ectatic antral vessels, associated with cirrhosis and connective tissue disease, typically in older men. Treated with repeated endoscopic thermal therapy every 4–8 weeks; TIPS does not help.
**Aorto-enteric fistula**: an aortic aneurysm or graft erodes into the third part of the duodenum. A small **‘herald’ bleed** comes hours to weeks before a massive, often fatal haemorrhage.
**Heyde syndrome**: bleeding angioectasias in a patient with aortic stenosis. Angioectasia is also linked with old age, CKD, cirrhosis and connective tissue disease.
Others: hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler–Weber–Rendu), pseudoxanthoma elasticum, blood dyscrasias.

blocks.text: In cirrhosis, **do not assume varices**: about 20% of suspected variceal bleeds actually come from non-variceal lesions, and peptic ulcer is more common in liver disease. Endoscopy must confirm the source.
**Isolated gastric varices** should make you look for **splenic vein thrombosis**; splenectomy cures bleeding gastric varices of that cause.

Quoted frequencies differ between books: Davidson gives peptic ulcer 35–50% and varices 2–9%, Kumar Essentials gives peptic ulcer ~50% and varices 10–20%, and Pocket Medicine gives peptic ulcer 20–60% and varices 4–20%. **Use Davidson’s figures**; every source puts peptic ulcer first.

blocks.note: Look at: the anatomical map of upper GI bleeding causes, each labelled with its approximate frequency.
Look at: GAVE — red stripes of ectatic vessels across the gastric antrum, with an argon plasma coagulation catheter.

sections.title: Lower GI and obscure bleeding: causes

blocks.text: Lower GI bleeding comes from **below the ligament of Treitz**: colon, anal canal or small bowel. Separate patients with **profuse acute** bleeding (red or maroon stool, often shock) from those with **chronic or subacute**, smaller-volume bleeding.

blocks.title: Key lesions
items: **Diverticular bleeding**: an artery erodes at the neck of a diverticulum. Bleeding nearly always stops by itself; if not, the segment is resected once angiography or colonoscopy has located it.
Diverticula are commoner on the **left**, yet bleeding diverticula are more often **right-sided**. Bleeding is painless, in older people; about 75% stop and about 20% recur.

**Angiodysplasia**: vascular malformations of the **proximal colon in the elderly**. Bleeding stops but tends to recur; colonoscopy shows vascular spots. First-choice treatment is endoscopic thermal ablation, with resection if bleeding persists.

**Ischaemic colitis**: inferior mesenteric artery occlusion in an elderly patient with widespread atherosclerosis — colicky abdominal pain with rectal bleeding. Diagnosed at colonoscopy; resection only if peritonitis develops.

blocks.title: Young patients and anorectal causes
items: **Meckel’s diverticulum**: ectopic gastric mucosa ulcerates into an artery. Think of it in a **child or adolescent** with profuse or recurrent bleeding. ‘Rule of 2s’: about 2% of people, within 2 feet of the ileocaecal valve, about 2 inches long, male:female 2:1.
A 99mTc-pertechnetate (Meckel’s) scan is sometimes positive, but the diagnosis is often made only at laparotomy.
**Haemorrhoids**: bright red blood during or after defecation. **Anal fissure**: fresh blood with **anal pain** on defecation. Together they cause most subacute or chronic lower GI bleeding.

blocks.text: **Massive** lower GI bleeding is uncommon and usually due to diverticular disease or ischaemic colitis; small bleeds from haemorrhoids and fissures are common. Most lower GI bleeds stop spontaneously and surgery is rarely required.

blocks.title: Obscure and chronic sources
items: **Obscure GI bleeding** means bleeding continues although OGD and colonoscopy are negative (about 5% of GI bleeds). Causes include Dieulafoy lesion, GAVE, small-bowel angiodysplasia, Crohn’s disease, aorto-enteric fistula, Meckel’s diverticulum and haemobilia.
Small-bowel sources: tumours, ulceration (Crohn’s, vasculitis, NSAIDs), angiodysplasia and Meckel’s diverticulum.
Worldwide, **hookworm** is the commonest cause of chronic GI blood loss. Varices rarely cause chronic loss because they bleed overtly.

blocks.text: Over the age of 40, treat a lower GI bleed as **colorectal cancer until proven otherwise** — even when haemorrhoids are present.

Step-Up calls diverticulosis the commonest source of GI bleeding in adults. Davidson and Kumar make **peptic ulcer** the commonest cause of serious GI bleeding overall; diverticular disease is the commonest cause of **severe acute lower** GI bleeding. Answer with Davidson.

blocks.note: Look at: lower GI bleeding causes placed at their usual colonic or anorectal sites (diverticula, carcinoma, polyps, colitis, haemorrhoids, fissure, angiodysplasia, Meckel’s).

sections.title: Haematemesis, melaena or blood per rectum?

blocks.title: Reading the bleed
rows: Upper GI, moderate to severe and possibly ongoing
Haemoglobin altered by digestive enzymes and gut bacteria over several hours
Proximal to the right colon (upper GI about 90%); occasionally small bowel or right colon
Fresh or maroon blood PR **with** shock
Blood passed too quickly to be altered
Consider a massive upper GI bleed
Bright red blood coating formed stool
Distal symptoms: urgency, straining, painful defecation

blocks.title: Rules of thumb
items: The **further from the rectum** the source, and the longer blood stays in the gut, the more likely melaena becomes.
Unaltered blood per rectum from an upper source needs a **massive** bleed and is almost always accompanied by **shock**.
About **5–10%** of patients with haematochezia have an upper GI source.
If melaena does come from the colon, the **ascending (right) colon** is the likeliest site.

blocks.text: A **rectal examination** belongs in the assessment of every suspected upper GI bleed: it shows whether stool is melaena, fresh blood or normal brown, and can reveal masses, haemorrhoids or fissures.
**Black stool is not always melaena.** Oral iron, bismuth, spinach, charcoal and liquorice can all darken stool — check the drug history and look for tarry consistency and smell.
Nasogastric lavage is **no longer routinely used** to decide whether bleeding is upper or lower; it has not been shown to improve outcomes.

sections.title: Clinical presentation, assessment and risk scores

blocks.title: History
items: Drugs: NSAIDs, aspirin, other antiplatelets (clopidogrel), anticoagulants.
Alcohol misuse, previous GI bleeding, known liver disease or coagulopathy; prior aortic surgery.
**Syncope** reflects hypotension from volume loss; **symptoms of anaemia** (fatigue, exertional breathlessness) point to chronic bleeding.
Associated features: abdominal pain, change in bowel habit, weight loss, vomiting before the bleed.

blocks.title: Examination
items: **Shock**: tachycardia, hypotension and oliguria in a cold, sweaty, often agitated patient.
**Stigmata of chronic liver disease**: jaundice, skin signs, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites.
**Comorbidity**: cardiorespiratory, cerebrovascular or renal disease — worsened by bleeding and raising the risk of endoscopy and surgery.
Marked abdominal tenderness with **peritonism** suggests perforation.
Rectal examination for stool colour, masses, haemorrhoids and fissures.

blocks.title: Estimating volume loss from vital signs
rows: Resting tachycardia (may be masked by β-blockers)
Postural change: systolic fall >20 mmHg or pulse rise >10 bpm

blocks.text: Hypotension may appear **late in fit young adults**, who compensate well; tachycardia and postural change already indicate moderate to severe loss.

About **85%** of upper GI bleeds stop spontaneously within 48 hours, but anyone with a significant bleed in the last 48 hours should be assessed in hospital. Pocket Medicine defines a **severe** bleed as shock, postural hypotension, a haemoglobin fall of 2 g/dL (haematocrit fall of 6%) or a need for at least 2 units of red cells — all need admission.

blocks.title: Rockall score
rows: Cardiac failure, IHD, other major comorbidity
Renal or liver failure, disseminated malignancy
Blood in upper GI tract, adherent clot, visible or spurting vessel

blocks.title: Using the scores
items: **Blatchford** uses urea, haemoglobin, BP and clinical markers but **no endoscopic findings**, so it can be done at the bedside; it predicts the need for intervention. A score of **2 or less** means low risk.
**Rockall**: the pre-endoscopy (clinical) part uses age, shock and comorbidity (maximum 7); the complete score adds diagnosis and stigmata (maximum 11) and predicts **rebleeding and death**.
Post-endoscopy Rockall 0: about 5% rebleed and no deaths; 3: 11% rebleed, 3% mortality; 8 or more: about 42% rebleed, 41% mortality.
A pre-endoscopy Rockall of 0–1 may allow discharge with outpatient endoscopy the next day, depending on local policy.

blocks.text: Low-risk cut-offs vary: Kumar allows discharge within 24 h with a pre-endoscopy Rockall of 0 and post-endoscopy <1; Kumar Essentials uses post-endoscopy ≤1; the Washington Manual uses a clinical score of 0 or complete score ≤2. Davidson’s low-risk marker is **Blatchford ≤2**.

sections.title: Investigations: acute, obscure and chronic bleeding

blocks.title: First blood tests
items: **FBC**: haemoglobin may be **normal straight after a sudden major bleed**, until haemodilution occurs. Low MCV suggests chronic loss and iron deficiency; low platelets hint at hypersplenism from chronic liver disease.

**Urea and electrolytes**: urea rises as digested blood is absorbed and metabolised by the liver. **High urea with normal creatinine implies a severe bleed** (US books use a BUN:creatinine ratio >36 for an upper source).
**LFTs and prothrombin time** when liver disease or anticoagulation is suspected.
**Cross-match**: Davidson says at least 2 units for a significant bleed; Kumar Essentials says at least 4 units for a large bleed (SBP <100 mmHg, pulse >100, cold peripheries, Hb <100 g/L).

blocks.title: Upper GI endoscopy
items: Done **after resuscitation**, ideally **within 24 h**; immediately after resuscitation if the patient is unstable. Gives a diagnosis in about **80%**.
**Stigmata of recent haemorrhage** (spurting vessel, active oozing, adherent clot, black spots) predict rebleeding and guide endoscopic therapy.
Take antral biopsies for _H. pylori_: a positive urease test can be trusted, but a **negative one is unreliable during bleeding**, so send histology.
In severe bleeding, IV erythromycin (about 250 mg) given 30 minutes before OGD clears blood from the stomach and improves the view.

blocks.title: Which test first?
rows: Upper GI endoscopy; colonoscopy if negative
Exclude an anorectal cause, then colonoscopy
Haematochezia with postural drop or shock
OGD first to exclude a brisk upper GI bleed

blocks.title: Lower GI work-up
items: Rectal examination and proctoscopy, then flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy; capsule endoscopy for the small bowel. Angiography has a low yield and is a last resort.
Colonoscopy finds the cause in more than 70%; colonoscopy within 24 h has not clearly beaten later colonoscopy for outcome.
Kumar: an **isolated** rectal bleed in someone **under 45** usually needs only rectal examination and flexible sigmoidoscopy.
Davidson: haemorrhoids are diagnosed by proctoscopy, but anyone **over 40** or with altered bowel habit needs colonoscopy to exclude coexisting colorectal cancer.

blocks.title: Major bleeding with a negative OGD and colonoscopy (Davidson)
rows: Urgent **CT mesenteric angiography** (finds bleeding >1 mL/min), then angiographic embolisation
Angiography negative or bleeding less severe
Push or double-balloon enteroscopy to see and treat the small bowel; capsule endoscopy can locate the source first

blocks.text: Detection thresholds differ: Davidson says CT mesenteric angiography usually finds bleeding above **1 mL/min**, whereas Pocket Medicine lists tagged red-cell scan ≥0.04 mL/min (rough location only), CT angiography ≥0.3 mL/min and catheter angiography ≥0.5 mL/min (pinpoints the vessel and allows embolisation). Quote Davidson in UK-style exams.

blocks.title: Chronic and occult bleeding
items: Occult bleeding (invisible to the eye) can reach **200 mL a day** and cause iron deficiency anaemia. The key cause is colorectal cancer, especially **caecal carcinoma**, which may give no GI symptoms.

In **men and postmenopausal women**, iron deficiency anaemia means GI blood loss until proven otherwise. Do a ‘top and tail’: OGD with **duodenal biopsies for coeliac disease** (even if serology was done) plus colonoscopy or CT colonography.
If both are clear, examine the small bowel: **capsule endoscopy** (yield 60–85%), then balloon-assisted enteroscopy to treat what it finds.

blocks.text: Faecal occult blood testing should **not** decide whether to image the gut, and has no place in the inpatient work-up of bleeding: tumours bleed intermittently, so a negative test excludes nothing. Its only role is screening people without symptoms.

blocks.note: Look at: a jejunal angiodysplasia found at enteroscopy in recurrent obscure bleeding.
Look at: small-bowel angiodysplastic lesions (arrowed) on video capsule endoscopy.

blocks.title: Resuscitation sequence
items: Large-bore IV access (Davidson: at least one cannula; Kumar: two).
Assess circulation, liver disease and comorbidity; send bloods and cross-match.
IV crystalloid to restore blood pressure; transfuse red cells when the patient is **actively bleeding with hypotension and tachycardia**.
Oxygen if shocked; nil by mouth until endoscopy; monitored bed or ITU according to severity.
Hourly pulse, blood pressure and urine output.
Suspected chronic liver disease: give broad-spectrum antibiotics.

blocks.text: **Transfusion thresholds differ.** Davidson ties transfusion to active bleeding with shock; Kumar cites a proposed restrictive threshold of **70 g/L** that is not yet universal; Pocket Medicine aims for Hb >7 g/dL (>8 with coronary disease). Over-transfusion risks heart failure in the elderly and may worsen variceal bleeding.

blocks.title: Antithrombotics and clotting
items: Stop NSAIDs, aspirin, clopidogrel and warfarin; discuss stopping antiplatelets **urgently with cardiology** because of stent thrombosis risk.
On warfarin and actively bleeding: give **prothrombin complex concentrate**.
Correct coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) and give platelets if the count is below 50 × 10⁹/L.
With coronary stents on dual antiplatelet therapy, aim to restart both drugs within **5–7 days**.

blocks.title: Peptic ulcer at endoscopy: finding → action
rows: Active bleeding, visible vessel, adherent clot
**Dual therapy**: adrenaline injection plus heater probe or clips; then IV PPI infusion for 72 h
Oozing in an otherwise stable patient
Endoscopic therapy, oral PPI, observe 24–48 h

blocks.title: Drug therapy
items: After endoscopic therapy for an actively bleeding ulcer or visible vessel: **IV omeprazole 80 mg then 8 mg/h for 72 h** — cuts rebleeding and the need for surgery.

Before endoscopy, Kumar Essentials gives this PPI regimen to high-risk patients (Rockall ≥4) whose endoscopy is delayed. Washington: a pre-endoscopy IV PPI lowers the share of patients with high-risk stigmata and the need for endoscopic therapy, yet an infusion beats IV bolus dosing on none of rebleeding, surgery or death in unselected patients.
PPIs work better than IV H2-receptor antagonists.
**Haemostatic powder (TC325)** sprayed at endoscopy is rescue therapy when standard methods fail.
Tranexamic acid: a meta-analysis showed lower mortality but no effect on rebleeding, surgery or transfusion.

blocks.title: When endoscopy fails
items: Davidson: **surgery** if endoscopy cannot stop active bleeding, or after **one rebleed in an elderly or frail** patient or **two in a younger, fitter** one.
In frail patients, **angiographic embolisation** can replace an operation; Kumar offers interventional radiology to everyone who rebleeds after endoscopy, with surgery if it is unavailable.
Duodenal ulcer surgery: under-running the bleeding vessel, with or without pyloroplasty.

Step-Up triggers for angiography or surgery: unstable despite fluids, blood, endotherapy and correction of clotting; a severe initial bleed, or a rebleed after endotherapy; bleeding beyond 24 h; or 5 units transfused in the first 4–6 h.
Before an emergency colectomy for unlocalised colonic bleeding, do an OGD to exclude a brisk upper source.

blocks.note: Look at: a duodenal ulcer bleeding actively (major stigma), then the same ulcer after adrenaline injection and heater probe.

blocks.title: Before endoscopy
items: Restore the circulation with blood and plasma — shock lowers liver blood flow and worsens liver function.

**Prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics for every cirrhotic with GI bleeding** (oral ciprofloxacin, IV cephalosporin or piperacillin–tazobactam): sepsis is common and antibiotics improve outcome. Washington gives 7 days of IV ceftriaxone.

**Terlipressin 2 mg IV four times daily** until bleeding stops, then 1 mg four times daily for up to 72 h. It lowers portal pressure and **reduces mortality**; use caution in ischaemic heart or peripheral vascular disease.
Octreotide (50–100 µg bolus then 25–50 µg/h) is the usual alternative where terlipressin is unavailable.
Lactulose and/or phosphate enema to prevent hepatic encephalopathy; a PPI to prevent peptic ulcers.
In severe bleeding, IV erythromycin (or metoclopramide 10 mg) before endoscopy.

blocks.title: At endoscopy
items: **Band ligation** is the usual first treatment and stops bleeding in about 80% (Davidson); it has largely replaced sclerotherapy.
Intubation protects the airway, helps the endoscopist and reduces aspiration during heavy bleeding.
**Gastric fundal varices** respond poorly to banding: inject **cyanoacrylate glue** or thrombin instead, accepting a risk of glue embolism to the lungs.

blocks.title: If endoscopic therapy fails
rows: Bridge to definitive therapy; almost always stops oesophageal and fundal variceal bleeding
For oesophageal (not gastric) varices; alternative bridge
Stent from portal to hepatic vein inside the liver; works for oesophageal and gastric varices; less rebleeding than endoscopy but no survival gain; encephalopathy risk
Kumar and Washington advise considering it early (for example in Child–Pugh C); reduces treatment failure and mortality
Radiological obliteration of gastric varices through a gastrorenal shunt

blocks.text: **Sengstaken tube safety**: intubate first; confirm the tube is in the stomach; inflate only the gastric balloon at first, with 200–250 mL of air, and **stop if the patient feels pain** (the balloon may be in the oesophagus — rupture risk). If the oesophageal balloon is needed, keep it ≤40 mmHg and deflate it for about 10 minutes every 3 hours.

**Terlipressin or octreotide?** Davidson and Kumar start terlipressin and keep octreotide for when terlipressin is unavailable; US texts (Pocket, Step-Up) start octreotide; Washington rates them as equally effective. For this course follow Davidson: **terlipressin plus antibiotics**.

blocks.note: Look at: the acute variceal bleeding algorithm — terlipressin and antibiotics, urgent endoscopy, banding, then tamponade or TIPSS if haemostasis fails.
Look at: the Sengstaken–Blakemore tube — gastric balloon, oesophageal balloon and the separate aspiration channels.

blocks.title: After a peptic ulcer bleed
items: Avoid NSAIDs from now on.
Test for _H. pylori_ and start eradication promptly; **confirm cure with a urea breath test or stool antigen test**.
Continue a PPI for 4 weeks to heal the ulcer; give long-term acid suppression if eradication fails.
Re-check whether antiplatelet therapy is really needed. If essential, co-prescribe a PPI; antithrombotics can restart once haemostasis is secure and a PPI is on board.

blocks.title: Gastroprotection
items: Give a PPI with aspirin or an NSAID if there is a previous ulcer or upper GI bleed **plus** a P2Y12 inhibitor or anticoagulant, or if two or more of: age over 60, steroids, dyspepsia.
COX-2-selective NSAIDs reduce ulcer bleeding but increase cardiovascular events.
PPIs reduce GI bleeding on dual antiplatelet therapy without a significant rise in cardiac events; pantoprazole interacts least with clopidogrel.

blocks.title: Varices: preventing the first and the next bleed
rows: Endoscopy when cirrhosis is diagnosed, repeated every 2 years
Non-selective β-blocker — propranolol 80–160 mg/day, or nadolol 40–240 mg/day — (aim for a 25% fall in heart rate), or carvedilol 6.25–12.5 mg/day; banding if a β-blocker is not tolerated
β-blocker **plus** an endoscopic banding programme until the varices are obliterated; PPI reduces bleeding from banding ulcers; TIPSS in selected patients
Cyanoacrylate glue prevents bleeding better than a β-blocker
Gastric varices from splenic vein thrombosis

blocks.text: Davidson gives two banding intervals: repeat banding **every 2–4 weeks** until varices are gone (acute section), but **12–24-week** sessions for the secondary-prevention programme. The examinable principle is the same: band repeatedly until obliteration, alongside a β-blocker.

blocks.title: Chronic bleeding and vascular lesions
items: Treat the cause; oral iron for the anaemia (IV occasionally); regular transfusion only as a last resort.
**Portal hypertensive gastropathy**: propranolol 80–160 mg/day first, TIPSS if that fails; oral iron to prevent anaemia.
Angiodysplasia: endoscopic thermal ablation; GAVE: repeated thermal therapy every 4–8 weeks.
Thalidomide may help refractory chronic bleeding from GI vascular malformations.

blocks.title: Prognosis
items: Hospital mortality is about **10%** (Davidson); Kumar quotes 5–12%, unchanged for years because patients are older with more comorbidity. Dedicated GI units achieve the best results.
Risk factors for death: age over 65, a severe first bleed, comorbidity, bleeding while already in hospital, emergency surgery, large transfusion needs, varices and endoscopic stigmata.
Variceal bleeding: overall mortality about 15%, but about 45% in Child–Pugh C.

blocks.note: Look at: TIPSS on X-ray — a stent running from the portal vein to the hepatic vein and on to the IVC.

cards.front: Commonest cause of acute upper GI haemorrhage, and its share (Davidson)?
Classic history of a Mallory–Weiss tear?
cards.back: Retching or vomiting (often alcoholic ‘dry heaves’) followed by haematemesis; a linear tear at the oesophagogastric junction that usually stops by itself.
Previous aortic graft or AAA plus a small ‘herald’ bleed, which precedes a massive haemorrhage hours to weeks later.

cards.front: Commonest cause of severe acute lower GI bleeding?
cards.back: Diverticular disease (artery eroded at the neck of a diverticulum); bleeding almost always stops spontaneously.

cards.front: Meckel’s diverticulum: who and which scan?
cards.back: A child or adolescent with profuse or recurrent lower GI bleeding; 99mTc-pertechnetate scan (often diagnosed only at laparotomy).

cards.front: What is melaena and where does it usually come from?
cards.back: Black, tarry stool of blood altered by enzymes and bacteria; usually an upper GI source (about 90%), occasionally small bowel or right colon.

cards.front: Fresh blood per rectum from an upper GI source — what almost always accompanies it?
cards.back: Shock: the bleed must be massive for blood to pass unaltered.

cards.front: Blatchford score threshold for low risk?
cards.back: A score of 2 or less (bedside, before endoscopy).
Pre-endoscopy: age, shock, comorbidity. Complete: adds endoscopic diagnosis and stigmata of recent haemorrhage.

cards.front: Raised urea with normal creatinine after haematemesis means?
cards.back: A severe (upper) bleed — digested blood is absorbed and metabolised to urea by the liver.

cards.front: Iron deficiency anaemia in a man or postmenopausal woman: first investigations?
cards.back: ‘Top and tail’: OGD with duodenal biopsies plus colonoscopy (or CT colonography); capsule endoscopy if both are normal.

cards.front: Life-threatening bleeding with normal OGD and colonoscopy: next test?
cards.back: Urgent CT mesenteric angiography, then angiographic embolisation.

cards.front: IV PPI regimen after endoscopic therapy for a bleeding ulcer?
cards.back: Omeprazole 80 mg IV bolus, then 8 mg/h for 72 hours.

cards.front: When is surgery indicated for a bleeding ulcer (Davidson)?
cards.back: Endoscopic haemostasis fails, or rebleeding once in an elderly/frail patient or twice in a younger fit one.

cards.front: Terlipressin dose in acute variceal bleeding?
cards.back: 2 mg IV four times daily until bleeding stops, then 1 mg four times daily for up to 72 hours.

cards.front: Which antimicrobial step is needed for every cirrhotic with GI bleeding?
cards.back: Prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. IV cephalosporin, oral ciprofloxacin) — sepsis is common and outcome improves.

cards.front: How is H. pylori eradication confirmed after an ulcer bleed?
cards.back: Urea breath test or faecal (stool) antigen test.
Non-selective β-blocker (propranolol 80–160 mg/day, nadolol, or carvedilol) titrated to a 25% heart-rate fall; banding if β-blocker not tolerated.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best option in the list. An option can fit several cases, or none.

items.stem: A 24-year-old medical student returns from a stag weekend of heavy drinking. After a night of repeated forceful vomiting of food and bile, he vomits a cupful of bright red blood. Pulse 88/min, BP 124/78 mmHg; no stigmata of liver disease.
items.explanation: Bleeding that **follows** repeated retching in a young drinker is the classic story for a linear tear at the oesophagogastric junction. Most stop spontaneously.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man had an open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair with a Dacron graft four years ago. Yesterday he vomited a small amount of fresh blood, which settled. Today he collapses with massive haematemesis and melaena.
items.explanation: Two steps: the prior aortic graft places the aorta next to the third part of the duodenum, and a minor **herald bleed** before a torrential one is the signature of a graft eroding into the bowel.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman with limited systemic sclerosis has had recurrent iron deficiency anaemia for a year with occasional black stools. Endoscopy shows parallel red stripes radiating across the gastric antrum.
items.explanation: Connective tissue disease, chronic iron deficiency and striped antral ectatic vessels (‘watermelon stomach’) point to GAVE, treated with repeated endoscopic thermal therapy.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best option in the list. An option can fit several cases, or none.

items.stem: A 13-year-old boy passes a large volume of painless dark red blood per rectum and becomes pale and tachycardic. He had a similar but smaller episode a year ago. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are normal.
items.explanation: Profuse, recurrent painless bleeding in an adolescent with normal endoscopies suggests ectopic gastric mucosa in a Meckel’s diverticulum ulcerating into an artery.

items.stem: A 79-year-old man with intermittent claudication and previous coronary bypass surgery develops sudden left-sided colicky abdominal pain followed within hours by bloody diarrhoea. He is not peritonitic.
items.explanation: Generalised atherosclerosis plus colicky pain then rectal bleeding indicates inferior mesenteric territory ischaemia; colonoscopy confirms and surgery is needed only if peritonitis develops.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman, recently constipated after childbirth, notices fresh blood on the toilet paper with a sharp, tearing pain on defecation that lasts for an hour afterwards.
items.explanation: Fresh blood **with anal pain** at defecation is the clue to a fissure; haemorrhoidal bleeding is typically painless.

items.stem: An 82-year-old woman with aortic stenosis has had three admissions in two years with painless bleeding per rectum that stopped on its own each time. Colonoscopy shows small flat red vascular spots in the caecum and ascending colon.
items.explanation: Two steps: recurrent self-limiting bleeding in an elderly patient with vascular spots in the **proximal** colon is angiodysplasia; the aortic stenosis completes Heyde syndrome.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man passes several large amounts of dark red blood and clots per rectum over 6 hours. He has had no haematemesis. Pulse 86/min, BP 132/80 mmHg lying and standing; he is warm and well perfused. He takes no regular medication and has no signs of chronic liver disease.
questions.leadIn: Which source is most likely?
questions.explanation: Dark blood and clots per rectum **without shock** most often come from the lower GI tract; in an older patient, diverticular disease is the commonest cause of acute lower GI bleeding. An upper source would need a massive bleed — almost always with shock — to reach the rectum unaltered.
whyNot: An upper bleed fast enough to pass red blood and clots per rectum is massive and almost always causes shock; he is haemodynamically stable.
Variceal bleeding is usually brisk with haematemesis, and he has no liver disease; unaltered PR blood from this source would come with shock.
Presents with haematemesis after retching, not isolated rectal bleeding.
Erosions cause haematemesis or melaena; they do not produce red blood and clots in a stable patient.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman started oral ferrous sulfate for menorrhagia three weeks ago. She reports formed, dark greenish-black stools. She has no abdominal pain or vomiting. Pulse 72/min, BP 118/74 mmHg. Haemoglobin is rising and urea is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation for her dark stools?
questions.explanation: Iron (like bismuth, charcoal, spinach and liquorice) darkens stool and mimics melaena. True melaena is tarry and foul-smelling; here the stool is formed, she is stable, Hb is rising and urea is normal, so no significant bleed has occurred.
whyNot: An ulcer bleed producing melaena would give tarry stool, often a raised urea and falling haemoglobin; none are present.
Occasionally causes melaena, but it is a disease of the elderly and her stable Hb argues against bleeding.
She has no liver disease, and varices bleed overtly with haematemesis and haemodynamic upset.
Causes slow occult loss with falling Hb in older patients; her Hb is rising on iron.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man who takes ibuprofen for back pain vomits dark material twice. On arrival: pulse 92/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, mild epigastric tenderness. Hb 128 g/L, urea 16 mmol/L, creatinine 82 µmol/L.
questions.leadIn: Which finding most strongly suggests that this is a severe bleed?
options: Raised blood urea with normal creatinine
questions.explanation: Blood in the gut is digested, absorbed and converted to urea by the liver, so a **high urea with normal creatinine** means a large volume of blood has entered the upper GI tract. Haemoglobin can be falsely reassuring early, because haemodilution has not yet occurred.
whyNot: Coffee grounds indicate blood altered by acid — typically a slower, less severe bleed than fresh red haematemesis.
A near-normal Hb straight after an acute bleed is unreliable; it falls only once haemodilution occurs.
Below the 100/min threshold; it does not score in Blatchford and is not a marker of severity on its own.
Mild tenderness fits an ulcer but says nothing about bleed size; only peritonism (suggesting perforation) changes management.

questions.stem: A foundation doctor is comparing the Glasgow–Blatchford and Rockall scores for a patient admitted with haematemesis who has not yet had endoscopy.
questions.leadIn: Which information is used by the complete Rockall score but not by the Blatchford score?
options: Endoscopic diagnosis and stigmata of recent haemorrhage
questions.explanation: Blatchford is built from bedside data — urea, haemoglobin, systolic BP, pulse, melaena, syncope, liver disease and cardiac failure — so it can be done before endoscopy. The complete Rockall adds **endoscopic diagnosis and stigmata** to age, shock and comorbidity to predict rebleeding and death.
whyNot: Urea is a Blatchford item (up to 6 points); Rockall does not use it.
Blatchford scores systolic BP directly; Rockall uses BP only within its ‘shock’ category, so this is not unique to Rockall.
Haemoglobin (sex-specific) is a Blatchford item; it is not part of Rockall.
Melaena scores 1 point in Blatchford; Rockall does not use it.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best option in the list. An option can fit several cases, or none.
options: OGD with duodenal biopsies plus colonoscopy

items.stem: A 66-year-old man is found to have Hb 92 g/L with MCV 71 fL during a routine check. He has no GI symptoms and no visible bleeding. He takes no medication.
items.explanation: Iron deficiency anaemia in a man is GI blood loss until proven otherwise: ‘top and tail’ him at one session, with duodenal biopsies for coeliac disease. Caecal cancer may cause no symptoms.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has had massive fresh bleeding per rectum. Urgent OGD and colonoscopy found no source. She has received 6 units of blood and remains hypotensive despite ongoing transfusion.
items.explanation: With life-threatening bleeding continuing after negative endoscopies, CT mesenteric angiography localises bleeding above about 1 mL/min and leads to embolisation.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man has had three episodes of melaena with iron deficiency over six months. OGD (with duodenal biopsies) and colonoscopy are normal. He is stable between episodes.
items.explanation: Two steps: normal upper and lower endoscopy plus recurrent overt bleeding means a likely small-bowel source; in a stable patient the next test is capsule endoscopy, followed by enteroscopy to treat.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man has noticed bright red blood on the paper after defecation for two months and has also had looser stools than usual. Proctoscopy shows grade 2 internal haemorrhoids.
items.explanation: Haemorrhoids are seen, but his age (over 40) and **altered bowel habit** mean coexisting colorectal cancer must be excluded by colonoscopy.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman taking naproxen presents with melaena and a pulse of 110/min. After resuscitation, endoscopy shows a duodenal ulcer with a non-bleeding visible vessel, which is treated with adrenaline injection and endoscopic clips.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate drug treatment now?
options: Oral omeprazole 20 mg daily and discharge
IV omeprazole 80 mg bolus then 8 mg/h for 72 hours
IV ranitidine 50 mg three times daily
IV terlipressin 2 mg four times daily
questions.explanation: A visible vessel is a major stigma of recent haemorrhage. After endoscopic dual therapy, a **72-hour high-dose IV PPI infusion** reduces rebleeding and the need for surgery.
whyNot: Oral PPI and discharge suits a clean-based, low-risk ulcer, not a visible vessel.
H2-receptor antagonists are less effective than PPIs in ulcer bleeding.
Terlipressin lowers portal pressure for variceal bleeding; it has no role in a peptic ulcer bleed.
Tranexamic acid has not been shown to reduce rebleeding or surgery and is not the standard post-endoscopy treatment.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old woman with heart failure and COPD had a bleeding gastric ulcer treated endoscopically with dual therapy two days ago. Today she has fresh haematemesis and her BP falls to 88/50 mmHg. Repeat endoscopy cannot achieve haemostasis. The surgeons consider her a very high operative risk.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue IV PPI and observe for a second rebleed
questions.explanation: Rebleeding once in an elderly, frail patient is an indication for definitive intervention. Where endoscopy fails and surgery is high risk, **angiographic embolisation** is an effective alternative.
whyNot: She is actively bleeding and shocked; discharge is unsafe.
TIPSS lowers portal pressure for variceal bleeding; it does nothing for an arterial ulcer bleed.
Balloon tamponade is a bridge for variceal bleeding, not for a bleeding gastric ulcer.
Waiting for a second rebleed applies to younger, fitter patients; in the elderly or frail, one rebleed warrants intervention.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best option in the list. An option can fit several cases, or none.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has torrential haematemesis. He is intubated and endoscopy shows a spurting oesophageal varix; banding fails because of poor views. The interventional radiology team cannot perform a shunt until the morning.
items.explanation: When endoscopic therapy fails, balloon tamponade nearly always controls variceal bleeding and acts as a **bridge** to definitive treatment such as TIPSS.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman with cirrhosis has haematemesis. Endoscopy shows active bleeding from large varices in the gastric fundus; the oesophagus is clear.
items.explanation: Banding works poorly on gastric fundal varices; injecting cyanoacrylate glue (or thrombin) into the varix is the endoscopic treatment of choice, with a small risk of glue embolism.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis presents with haematemesis. LFTs are normal and there are no stigmata of liver disease. Endoscopy shows isolated gastric varices; CT shows an occluded splenic vein.
items.explanation: Two steps: isolated gastric varices with normal liver function point to splenic vein thrombosis (a complication of pancreatitis), and **splenectomy** cures the bleeding in that situation.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man with known cirrhosis arrives with haematemesis, pulse 118/min and BP 92/60 mmHg. IV access is secured, blood is cross-matched and broad-spectrum antibiotics are given. Endoscopy is arranged for the next hour.
items.explanation: Before endoscopy, suspected variceal bleeding is treated with a vasopressin analogue to lower portal pressure; terlipressin reduces mortality. Antibiotics have already been given.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man recovered from a bleeding duodenal ulcer. Gastric histology confirmed _Helicobacter pylori_ and he completed a course of eradication therapy.
questions.leadIn: Which test should be used to confirm successful eradication?
options: Repeat rapid urease test on biopsy during active bleeding
questions.explanation: After an ulcer bleed, eradication must be **confirmed**, using a urea breath test or a faecal antigen test.
whyNot: Serology is not one of the tests the textbooks recommend for confirming cure; urea breath or stool antigen tests are used.
A negative urease test during bleeding is unreliable, and he is no longer bleeding — this does not confirm cure.
Imaging may show an ulcer but cannot detect H. pylori.
Gastrin is measured for suspected gastrinoma, not to confirm H. pylori eradication.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with cirrhosis had her first oesophageal variceal bleed controlled with terlipressin and band ligation. She is now stable and ready to plan discharge.
questions.leadIn: Which strategy best prevents a further variceal bleed?
options: Non-selective β-blocker plus an endoscopic banding programme
β-blocker alone with endoscopy every 2 years
No treatment until the next bleed
questions.explanation: Secondary prevention combines a **β-blocker** with **repeated banding sessions** until the varices are obliterated (TIPSS is reserved for selected patients). A PPI reduces bleeding from banding ulcers.
whyNot: 2-yearly endoscopy is for screening cirrhotics who have not bled; after a bleed she needs active banding as well.
Terlipressin is an acute IV treatment given for up to 72 hours, not for long-term prevention.
Antibiotics prevent infection during the acute bleed but do not prevent varices from rebleeding.
Variceal bleeding often recurs without preventive therapy, and each bleed carries high mortality.

questions.theme: Drug and blood-product treatment in acute GI bleeding
questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best option in the list. An option can fit several cases, or none.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation has melaena with pulse 112/min and BP 94/58 mmHg. INR is 4.8. He is still actively bleeding.
items.explanation: Warfarin with active bleeding is reversed with prothrombin complex concentrate as part of resuscitation.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman with cirrhosis has haematemesis and has been started on terlipressin. She is afebrile and her white cell count is normal.
items.explanation: Every cirrhotic with GI bleeding needs **prophylactic** antibiotics — sepsis is common and antibiotics improve outcome even without signs of infection.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man has heavy ongoing haematemesis; the stomach is likely to be full of clot. The endoscopist wants a clearer view at the procedure in 30 minutes.
items.explanation: IV erythromycin given about 30 minutes before endoscopy speeds gastric emptying of blood and clot and improves the diagnostic yield.

items.stem: Two days after a variceal bleed, a 58-year-old man with cirrhosis becomes drowsy and confused, with a flapping tremor. He is apyrexial and his bleeding has stopped.
items.explanation: Two steps: a GI bleed in cirrhosis can tip the patient into hepatic encephalopathy, and lactulose (or a phosphate enema) is part of variceal-bleed management to prevent and treat it.

questions.stem: An audit of all adults admitted with acute upper GI haemorrhage to a UK district general hospital over one year is being planned.
questions.leadIn: Which cause would be expected to be the most frequent?
questions.explanation: Peptic ulcer accounts for about 35–50% of acute upper GI bleeds and is the leading cause of serious bleeding. Erosions (10–20%) and oesophagitis (10%) follow; varices make up 2–9% in Davidson’s figures.
whyNot: Common (10–20%) but less frequent than peptic ulcer.
Only 2–9% in Davidson, although they carry a high mortality.
About 5% of upper GI bleeds.
About 10%, usually with a hiatus hernia.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man vomits about a litre of fresh blood 40 minutes before arrival. He is pale and sweaty, pulse 124/min and BP 90/60 mmHg. His haemoglobin is 138 g/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the best explanation for the normal haemoglobin?
options: The bleed must be from the lower GI tract
Iron stores are mobilised to the marrow immediately
The spleen releases stored red cells
The laboratory sample was taken from a drip arm
questions.explanation: Immediately after a sudden major bleed the patient loses whole blood, so the **concentration** of Hb is unchanged until fluid shifts and resuscitation dilute it. Judge severity by haemodynamics, not the first Hb.
whyNot: He vomited fresh blood — clearly an upper source — and the site of bleeding does not explain the normal Hb.
New red-cell production takes days; it cannot correct Hb within an hour.
This is not the mechanism; the normal Hb reflects lack of dilution.
A drip-arm sample would falsely **lower** the Hb, not keep it normal.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old man has had several self-limiting episodes of painless bleeding per rectum over a year, with iron deficiency anaemia. Colonoscopy shows multiple flat vascular spots in the caecum, one of which is oozing.
questions.leadIn: What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: This is **angiodysplasia** of the proximal colon in an elderly patient. Endoscopic thermal ablation is the treatment of choice; resection is reserved for bleeding that continues.
whyNot: Resection is kept for bleeding that persists despite endoscopic therapy.
Propranolol treats portal hypertensive bleeding, not colonic angiodysplasia.
Acid suppression has no effect on colonic vascular malformations.
Used for ulcerative colitis, which this is not.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old postmenopausal woman has fatigue. Hb is 94 g/L, MCV 70 fL and ferritin is low. She has no GI symptoms. Coeliac serology was negative last year.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate investigation?
options: Gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies and colonoscopy
Faecal occult blood test to decide whether to investigate
Oral iron and repeat blood count in 3 months
Capsule endoscopy as the first test
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency in a postmenopausal woman is GI blood loss until proven otherwise; the main fears are gastric or right-colon cancer and coeliac disease. Investigate upper and lower tract at one session, taking **duodenal biopsies even with negative serology**.
whyNot: Bleeding is intermittent, so a negative FOB test excludes nothing; it should not decide whether to image.
Treating without investigating risks missing a silent caecal or gastric cancer.
Capsule endoscopy follows a normal OGD and colonoscopy.
Reserved for severe, life-threatening active bleeding, not chronic occult loss.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presents with melaena. He has no syncope, liver disease or heart failure. Pulse 92/min, systolic BP 115 mmHg. Blood urea 7.2 mmol/L, haemoglobin 125 g/L.
questions.leadIn: What is his modified Glasgow–Blatchford score?
questions.explanation: Work through each item. **Urea** 7.2 mmol/L sits in the 6.5–8 band = **2**. **Hb** 125 g/L in a man (120–129) = **1**. **Systolic BP** 115 (>109) = 0. **Pulse** 92 (<100) = 0. **Melaena** = **1**. No syncope, hepatic disease or cardiac failure = 0. Total = 2 + 1 + 1 = **4**. As this is above 2, he is not low risk and needs inpatient endoscopy.
whyNot: Counts only the urea band and misses the haemoglobin and melaena points.
Forgets that melaena itself scores 1, or that Hb 120–129 g/L in a man scores 1.
Adds one point that does not apply — for example for the pulse of 92 (only 100 or more scores) or the systolic of 115 (only below 110 scores).
Adds points for both pulse and blood pressure, although a pulse of 92 and a systolic of 115 both score 0.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with cirrhosis continues to bleed from oesophageal varices after banding and terlipressin. TIPSS is not available tonight, so a Sengstaken–Blakemore tube is planned.
questions.leadIn: Which step is correct?
options: Fill the gastric balloon with 500 mL of air
Continue inflating the gastric balloon if the patient reports pain
Leave the oesophageal balloon inflated continuously for 24 hours
questions.explanation: Reason through the hazards: (1) a bleeding, often encephalopathic patient risks **aspiration**, so the airway is secured with endotracheal intubation first; (2) the tube goes through the mouth and gastric position is confirmed; (3) only the **gastric balloon** is inflated initially, with **200–250 mL** of air and gentle traction — this usually controls bleeding; (4) pain during inflation means the balloon may be in the oesophagus, so stop (rupture risk); (5) if the oesophageal balloon is needed, keep it ≤40 mmHg and deflate it about 10 minutes every 3 hours. The tube is a bridge to definitive therapy.
whyNot: The gastric balloon is inflated first and usually controls bleeding alone; the oesophageal balloon is added only if bleeding continues.
The recommended volume is 200–250 mL.
Pain suggests the balloon is in the oesophagus; inflation must stop because of rupture risk.
It must be deflated for about 10 minutes every 3 hours to avoid mucosal damage.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman reports bright red blood on the toilet paper after defecation for six weeks. There is no pain. She has no change in bowel habit. Proctoscopy shows bleeding internal haemorrhoids.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Rubber band ligation of haemorrhoids only
questions.explanation: Step 1: the pattern (bright red, during or after defecation, painless) fits haemorrhoids, and proctoscopy confirms them. Step 2: finding haemorrhoids does not exclude a second lesion. Davidson advises colonoscopy for anyone presenting **over 40** (or with altered bowel habit) to exclude **coexisting colorectal cancer**. Step 3: she is 52, so she needs colonoscopy. Note the different cut-off in Kumar (flexible sigmoidoscopy alone for isolated bleeding under 45) — she is over both thresholds.
whyNot: At 52, a lower GI bleed must be treated as possible colorectal cancer until proven otherwise.
Treating the haemorrhoids without examining the colon could miss a coexisting cancer.
She already has visible bleeding; FOB testing has no role in deciding whether to image.
Bright red blood coating stool after defecation is anorectal or colonic, not upper GI.

questions.theme: Diagnosing the source of GI blood loss
questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best option in the list. An option can fit several cases, or none.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis has iron deficiency anaemia but no visible bleeding. Endoscopy shows no varices; the gastric fundus and body have a diffuse mosaic, snakeskin-like pattern with punctate red spots.
items.explanation: A snakeskin mucosal pattern in portal hypertension is congestive gastropathy, which more often causes chronic minor bleeding and iron deficiency than acute haemorrhage.

items.stem: A 77-year-old woman has iron deficiency anaemia, weight loss of 4 kg and no abdominal symptoms. Gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies is normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: unexplained iron deficiency in an older patient with a normal OGD points to the colon, and caecal carcinoma typically bleeds occultly without GI symptoms.

items.stem: A 26-year-old agricultural labourer from a rural tropical region, who works barefoot, has chronic iron deficiency anaemia. OGD and colonoscopy are normal and he has no overt bleeding.
items.explanation: Hookworm is the commonest cause of chronic GI blood loss worldwide and should be considered in someone from an endemic area with iron deficiency and normal endoscopy.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man has sudden massive haematemesis with shock. At the first endoscopy, blood obscures the view and no ulcer is found. At repeat endoscopy a single pulsating vessel is seen protruding through otherwise normal mucosa in the gastric fundus.
items.explanation: A large submucosal artery protruding through normal fundal mucosa, causing torrential bleeding and missed at first endoscopy, is a Dieulafoy lesion.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis has recurrent melaena and transfusion-dependent anaemia. OGD and colonoscopy are normal; capsule endoscopy shows several small flat red lesions in the jejunum.
items.explanation: Bleeding angioectasias with aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome) are a classic cause of obscure small-bowel bleeding found on capsule endoscopy.

questions.theme: Decisions in acute non-variceal upper GI bleeding
questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best option in the list. An option can fit several cases, or none.
options: Discharge with outpatient endoscopy the next day

items.stem: A 23-year-old man vomited a few streaks of blood after a bout of retching. Pulse 76/min, BP 128/80 mmHg, Hb 146 g/L, urea 4.8 mmol/L; no melaena, syncope, liver disease or heart failure.
items.explanation: His Blatchford score is 0 (and pre-endoscopy Rockall 0), so he is low risk and can be discharged with outpatient endoscopy.

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman has repeated haematemesis, pulse 128/min and BP 82/50 mmHg despite 2 L of crystalloid and 2 units of blood. She is on ITU.
items.explanation: Unstable patients with severe upper GI bleeding should be endoscoped immediately after resuscitation rather than waiting up to 24 hours.

items.stem: At endoscopy a 58-year-old man has a 1 cm duodenal ulcer with a clean white base and no stigmata of recent haemorrhage. He is haemodynamically stable.
items.explanation: A clean-based ulcer is low risk for rebleeding: oral PPI and early discharge, plus H. pylori testing.

items.stem: A 41-year-old fit man has had a bleeding duodenal ulcer treated endoscopically twice; he now rebleeds a second time and repeat endoscopy fails. Interventional radiology is not available.
items.explanation: Two steps: in a younger, fitter patient, surgery follows a second rebleed; with no radiology available, the operation for a duodenal ulcer is under-running of the vessel, with or without pyloroplasty.

items.stem: At endoscopy, a gastric ulcer is oozing diffusely. Adrenaline injection and a heater probe have failed to stop it, and clips cannot be positioned.
items.explanation: An inert haemostatic powder sprayed through the endoscope is the rescue therapy when standard dual therapy fails.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with a bleeding duodenal ulcer has been resuscitated and is haemodynamically stable after endoscopic therapy. He has no ischaemic heart disease. The team adopts the restrictive red-cell transfusion strategy cited by Kumar & Clark.
questions.leadIn: Below which haemoglobin concentration would further red cells be given?
questions.explanation: Kumar & Clark quote a proposed restrictive threshold of **70 g/L** (Pocket Medicine: >7 g/dL, or >8 g/dL with coronary disease). Over-transfusion risks heart failure in the elderly and may worsen variceal bleeding. Davidson’s rule is clinical: transfuse when actively bleeding with hypotension and tachycardia.
whyNot: Too low; this is below the restrictive threshold the sources describe.
A liberal target that risks over-transfusion; restrictive strategies use about 70 g/L (80 g/L with coronary disease).
Over-transfusion target; it may cause fluid overload, especially in older patients.
Far above any recommended threshold and risks heart failure.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with hyperemesis gravidarum vomits bright red blood after several hours of forceful retching. Endoscopy shows a single linear mucosal tear.
questions.leadIn: Where is this lesion found?
questions.explanation: A Mallory–Weiss tear is a linear mucosal laceration at the **oesophagogastric junction**, caused by a sudden rise in intra-abdominal pressure during retching. Most stop bleeding spontaneously.
whyNot: Typical site for GAVE and gastric ulcers, not Mallory–Weiss tears.
Typical site of duodenal ulcers.
Where an aortic graft or aneurysm can erode to form an aorto-enteric fistula.
Usual site of Dieulafoy lesions and gastric varices.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best option in the list. An option can fit several cases, or none.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with polymyalgia rheumatica and osteoarthritis takes two drugs that, in combination, have a synergistic effect on the risk of peptic ulcer bleeding, although one of them alone barely raises the risk.
items.explanation: Steroids alone add little bleeding risk, but combined with an NSAID they raise it synergistically.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man with cirrhosis and severe peripheral vascular disease has a variceal bleed. The team uses a drug that lowers portal pressure and reduces mortality, but must monitor closely because its vasoconstrictor effect may cause limb ischaemia.
items.explanation: Terlipressin lowers portal pressure and mortality in variceal bleeding; its vasoconstriction calls for caution in ischaemic heart or peripheral vascular disease.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman has transfusion-dependent anaemia from multiple small-bowel vascular malformations that have kept bleeding despite repeated endoscopic ablation. A drug option is considered.
items.explanation: Thalidomide may help refractory chronic bleeding from GI vascular malformations.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man on aspirin and clopidogrel after a coronary stent had an ulcer bleed. A PPI is prescribed for gastroprotection, choosing the agent with the least interaction with clopidogrel.
items.explanation: Two steps: a PPI is indicated with dual antiplatelets after a bleed, and among PPIs pantoprazole has the least pharmacodynamic interaction with clopidogrel.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis, ascites and spider naevi vomits 500 mL of fresh blood. Pulse 116/min, BP 96/58 mmHg. IV access is secured and blood is being cross-matched; endoscopy is planned within the hour.
questions.leadIn: Which treatment should be started now?
options: Fresh frozen plasma to normalise the INR
questions.explanation: Suspected variceal bleeding in cirrhosis: start a vasoactive drug (**terlipressin**, which reduces mortality) and **prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics** before urgent endoscopy and band ligation.
whyNot: A PPI is used in variceal management but does not lower portal pressure; on its own it is inadequate.
β-blockers are for primary and secondary prevention, not for a shocked patient who is actively bleeding.
TIPSS is a rescue when endoscopic therapy fails, not the first step.
In cirrhosis the INR is a poor guide to bleeding risk; the priorities are vasoactive drugs, antibiotics and endoscopy.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man had an endovascular aortic graft for an abdominal aortic aneurysm three years ago. He passed a single small melaena stool yesterday, which stopped. Today he is stable, Hb 121 g/L. He takes no NSAIDs.
questions.leadIn: Which diagnosis is the most important to exclude urgently?
questions.explanation: A previous aortic graft plus a minor, self-limiting **herald bleed** must raise suspicion of an aorto-enteric fistula into the third part of the duodenum. A massive, often fatal bleed may follow within hours to weeks, so CT angiography and surgery should be urgent.
whyNot: The commonest cause overall, but the graft history makes a fistula the lesion that must not be missed.
Needs a history of retching or vomiting, which he does not have.
There is no history or sign of liver disease.
Usually causes slow occult loss and weight loss, not the herald-bleed pattern after aortic surgery.

ospe.identify: Gastric antral vascular ectasia (‘watermelon stomach’): red stripes of ectatic vessels in the antrum; treated with argon plasma coagulation or other thermal therapy.
Duodenal ulcer with active bleeding (a major stigma of recent haemorrhage); after adrenaline injection and heater probe, haemostasis — ‘dual therapy’.
Jejunal angiodysplasia at enteroscopy — a cause of recurrent obscure GI bleeding after a negative OGD and colonoscopy.
Small-bowel angiodysplastic lesions on video capsule endoscopy — the next test after a normal OGD and colonoscopy in obscure bleeding.
Sengstaken–Blakemore tube: gastric balloon (inflated first, 200–250 mL air), oesophageal balloon and the gastric and oesophageal aspiration channels.
TIPSS on X-ray: a stent from the portal vein through the liver into the hepatic vein and IVC, lowering portal pressure in refractory variceal bleeding.
